questions.q: What two methods does the lesson's `QuantumBackend` abstract base class require every concrete backend to implement?
options: connect() and disconnect()
run(circuit, shots) and name()
build() and measure()
install() and configure()
questions.explain: The shared interface defines run(circuit, shots) -> dict (execute and return counts) and name() -> str (a human-readable identifier for logging/reproducibility), which both LocalSimulatorBackend and IBMHardwareBackend implement identically.

questions.q: Why does `run_bell_experiment(backend, shots)` work unmodified whether it's given a `LocalSimulatorBackend` or an `IBMHardwareBackend`?
options: Because both classes happen to have identical internal code
Because the function depends only on the shared QuantumBackend interface and never imports AerSimulator or QiskitRuntimeService directly
Because Qiskit automatically converts between simulator and hardware backends
Because the function ignores the backend parameter entirely
questions.explain: Because run_bell_experiment is written against the abstract interface rather than a concrete backend class, swapping which concrete implementation is passed in requires no change to the function itself -- the direct payoff of Lesson 10's dependency injection.

questions.q: What does `backend_from_config()` enable, combined with Lesson 2's configuration-file pattern?
options: Choosing which backend to use based on external configuration (e.g. a CI env var or config file) rather than hardcoding it in algorithm code
Automatically detecting the fastest backend at runtime
Running on all backends simultaneously
Bypassing the need for an abstract interface entirely
questions.explain: backend_from_config() reads a config value (like backend_type: 'simulator' vs 'ibm_hardware') and returns the matching concrete backend -- letting CI and production select different backends through configuration alone, with the exact same deployed code.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue against adding `get_calibration_data()` to the shared `QuantumBackend` interface?
options: Because calibration data doesn't exist on any backend
Because a simulator has no meaningful calibration data, so forcing it into the shared contract would require simulators to fake a meaningless return value -- a capability-leakage mistake
Because calibration data is classified information
Because Python ABCs cannot have more than two abstract methods
questions.explain: Calibration data is a real-hardware-specific concept with no meaningful simulator equivalent. Forcing it into the shared interface would require every backend, including simulators, to implement it somehow -- the capability-leakage problem the lesson warns against.

questions.q: Where does the lesson recommend exposing hardware-specific capabilities like queue position or calibration data instead of the shared interface?
options: Nowhere -- those capabilities should simply not be accessible in code
Through a separate, optional interface or a hardware-specific subclass that algorithm code reaches for only when it explicitly knows it's targeting real hardware
By adding them to the shared interface anyway and returning None on simulators
By requiring all simulators to also implement a fake hardware queue
questions.explain: The lesson recommends a separate optional interface or hardware-specific subclass for capabilities that don't generalize across all backend types, keeping the shared QuantumBackend contract limited to what every implementation can genuinely support.
